elements.content:
• What is HTML and why it matters

• Learning objectives for the next 20 minutes

• Course structure and how to follow along

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and today we’re kicking off our journey into HTML, the language that builds every web page you visit.

First, let’s answer the question: what is HTML and why does it matter? HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the foundation of web content—think of it as the skeleton that gives structure to everything you see online.

In the next twenty minutes we’ll cover three learning objectives: understand the role of HTML, identify the basic building blocks like tags and elements, and see how to create a simple page that you can view in any browser.
I’ll also walk you through the course structure: we’ll start with concepts, move to live coding demos, and finish with a quick hands‑on exercise you can try right now.
If you follow along on your own device, you’ll be able to build a personal webpage by the end of this session—so keep your editor open and let’s dive in!

Remember, <h1> is the most important heading and <h6> the least; using them in order helps both users and search engines understand the page structure.

elements.content:
• Anchor tag: <a href="URL">text</a>

• Image tag: <img src="path" alt="description">

• Use descriptive alt text for accessibility

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into today’s topic: Links and Images. These two HTML elements are the building blocks that make a webpage interactive and visually engaging.
First, the anchor tag creates a hyperlink. The basic syntax is text. The href attribute points to the destination, and the text between the tags is what the user clicks.
Notice the quotation marks around the URL and how the closing tag wraps up the link.

Next, the image tag embeds a picture: . The src attribute tells the browser where the image file lives, while the alt attribute provides a text description for accessibility and for cases where the image can’t load.
Remember, good alt text should be concise yet descriptive—think of it as a caption for users who rely on screen readers.
To recap, we covered how to create clickable links with the tag and how to embed images with the tag, emphasizing the importance of descriptive alt text for accessibility.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a level‑1 heading?
questions.analysis: The <h1> tag defines a top‑level heading. <heading> is not a valid HTML tag, <title> is for the document title shown in the browser tab, and <head> contains metadata, not visible headings.

Place the image file inside a <picture> element without a src attribute.

Close the tag with a separate closing tag.

questions.analysis: Correct: is the standard way to embed an image, and an alt attribute is required for accessibility. is used for responsive images but still requires with src. is a void element and must not have a closing tag.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, it's time to see how well you've grasped the basic HTML tags we just covered. This short quiz will check your understanding of headings and embedding images, so read each question carefully and choose the best answer.

Remember, a level‑1 heading is created with the <h1> tag. It's the most important heading on a page and signals the main title to both browsers and search engines. The other tags like <heading>, <title>, and <head> serve different purposes and won't produce a visible heading in the page body.

When you embed an image, the correct approach is to use the tag with a src attribute that points to the image file, and always include an alt attribute for accessibility. The tag is self‑closing, so you don't add a separate tag. Using a element is useful for responsive images, but it still requires inside it with a src attribute.

elements.content:
• Ordered list <ol> with <li>

• Unordered list <ul> with <li>

• Nest lists for hierarchy

actions.text: Okay class, let's dive into lists in HTML. We'll start with the big idea: ordered and unordered lists let us structure information neatly on a page.
First, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag, and each item is wrapped in an <li>. This creates a numbered sequence—perfect for steps or rankings.
Next, an unordered list uses <ul> with <li> items, giving you bullet points ideal for simple collections.
Finally, you can nest lists inside each other to create hierarchical outlines—just place a new <ul> or <ol> inside an <li>.
To recap, we covered the <ol> tag for ordered lists, <ul> for unordered lists, and how nesting builds structure. Any questions before we move on?

• Header vs. data cells

• Use <th> for headings

• Add <caption> for accessibility
Provide a concise caption describing the table’s purpose.

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into tables. This slide is all about the basics of HTML tables and why they’re useful for structuring data.
Here’s a simple 2 × 2 table built with the <table>, <tr>, <th>, and <td> tags. Notice how each row is defined by <tr> and the cells inside are either header cells <th> or data cells <td>.
A key point: use <th> for header cells and <td> for regular data cells. Header cells help browsers and assistive technologies understand the structure of your table.
Finally, always add a concise caption with the <caption> element and use the scope attribute on <th> to improve accessibility. That way, screen readers can convey the table’s purpose clearly.
That covers the fundamentals of HTML tables—structure, header vs. data cells, and a quick accessibility tip. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Form container <form>

• Input elements: <input>, <textarea>, <button>

• Label association with <label>

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into our Forms Overview. Forms are how we collect information from visitors on a web page.
First, the form container itself uses the <form> tag. Think of it like a box that holds all the fields you want your user to fill out.
Inside that box, we place input elements such as <input> for single‑line data, <textarea> for multi‑line text, and <button> to submit the form.
Finally, we use <label> to associate each input with a readable description, which improves accessibility and lets users know exactly what to enter.
That’s the core of HTML forms—container, inputs, and labels. With these three pieces, you can start building simple contact forms or surveys right away.

elements.content:
• Sectioning elements: header, nav, main, section, article, footer

• Improves SEO and assists screen‑readers

• Choose tags that reflect content purpose

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Semantic HTML and see how it helps us build clearer, more accessible web pages.
Using semantic tags matters because they give meaning to the structure of our document, which search engines and screen‑reader tools can understand more easily.

Here are the main sectioning elements: <header> for the top navigation or banner, <nav> for groups of links, <main> for the core content, <section> for thematic groupings, <article> for self‑contained pieces, and <footer> for closing information.
When you choose the right tag, you improve SEO, make your site more accessible, and keep your code organized for future maintenance.
So remember: think about the purpose of each piece of content and match it with the most appropriate semantic element.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create an ordered (numbered) list?
questions.analysis: The <ol> tag defines an ordered list where items are automatically numbered. <ul> creates an unordered (bulleted) list, <li> defines a list item, and <dl> defines a description list.

questions.question: Select all HTML elements that are considered semantic markup (choose all that apply).
questions.analysis: <section> and <header> convey meaning about the structure of the page, making them semantic. <div> and <span> are generic containers without intrinsic meaning, so they are non‑semantic.

questions.question: Which HTML element is most appropriate for grouping related form controls together?
questions.analysis: <fieldset> groups related controls within a form and can include a <legend> for description. <form> is the overall container for form data, <label> associates text with a control, and <section> is for generic document sections.

actions.text: Now let's check what we've learned about HTML structure with a quick quiz. Remember, each tag has a specific purpose, so think about what each element is meant to represent before you choose.

For the first question, recall that ordered lists display items with numbers. Which tag creates that kind of list? Keep in mind the tag that directly defines the list itself, not the individual items.

The second question asks you to spot semantic markup. Semantic tags describe the meaning of their content, whereas generic containers like <div> or <span> don’t convey that meaning. Consider which options give the browser and developers clear information about the page structure.
The third question focuses on grouping related form controls. Think about the tag that visually and logically groups fields together, often adding a caption with a <legend> element.

elements.content:
• Consistent indentation for readability

• Meaningful alt text for images

• Explore validation tools & online editors

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's wrap up with some best practices and next steps for your HTML journey.
First, keep your indentation consistent. Clean, orderly code is much easier to read and debug.
Second, always add meaningful alt text to images. It improves accessibility and helps search engines understand your content.
Finally, explore validation tools like the W3C Markup Validator and online editors such as CodePen or Replit. They give instant feedback and keep you on the right track.
Take a few minutes today to apply these habits in a small project—maybe a personal homepage for yourself. Practice makes perfect, and you'll see your confidence grow with every line of code.
Great work today, everyone! Keep experimenting, and I'll see you in the next session.
